findings.title: Managed write-lease validation is split from the state mutation that admits the request
findings.description: The Online adapter authorizes a managed write against a snapshot loaded before `mutateState()`, then increments in-flight state in a later serialized mutation. A concurrent lease-confirmation refresh, mode flip, or logout can revoke that lease after the read-side check but before the request is admitted, so one stale write can still cross the single-writer fence.
findings.snippet: const lease = state.leases[handle]; if (isWrite && envelope.loginMode === STCONTROL_MODES.MANAGED && (!lease || ...)) { return response.status(409)... } await mutateState(current => { ... current.sessions[envelope.sessionId] = session; });
findings.recommendation: Move lease/gate/session validation and the in-flight increment into one `mutateState()` transaction that returns an allow/deny decision. Do not call `next()` unless the same serialized critical section has rechecked the current lease snapshot and recorded the request as in flight.
findings.impact: This breaks the architecture's single-writer invariant during failover and recovery. A revoked or expired controller lease can still admit one more managed mutation, which is exactly the overlap the activity-lease protocol is supposed to prevent.

findings.title: Managed-to-independent session promotion only updates the browser envelope, not the durable session state
findings.description: When the node enters independent mode, the adapter rewrites `request.session.stcontrol` to `independent`, but the persisted session record is reused unchanged inside `mutateState()`. Existing managed sessions therefore remain durably labeled as managed even after takeover, so later draining/reconciliation logic reads the wrong role and misses independent-write bookkeeping.
findings.snippet: if (state.mode === STCONTROL_MODES.INDEPENDENT && envelope.loginMode !== STCONTROL_MODES.INDEPENDENT) { ... envelope.loginMode = STCONTROL_MODES.INDEPENDENT; ... } ... const session = current.sessions[envelope.sessionId] ?? { handle, loginMode: envelope.loginMode, ... };
findings.recommendation: Whenever the request envelope is promoted to `independent`, overwrite the durable `current.sessions[sessionId]` role, activity epoch, and controller generation in the same mutation. Add a regression test that starts from a managed session, flips to independent, performs a write, and asserts both `activeIndependentSessions` and `pendingUserSyncs` advance before draining.
findings.impact: The recovered controller can be told there are zero independent sessions or pending syncs even after the browser has already switched to disaster-write mode. That can reopen managed mode too early, or incorrectly block a legitimate draining session because the agent's durable control-mode view never observed the promotion.

findings.title: Recovery gate is process-local and not revalidated inside repair/backup scheduling transactions
findings.description: The controller checks `checkNewOperations()` before launching storage-repair or controller-backup work, but the subsequent store claim/schedule transactions do not re-assert control-plane readiness. If a heartbeat closes the gate after the in-memory check and before the DB claim completes, the same scheduler tick can still create a new workflow while recovery mode is already supposed to reject new operations.
findings.snippet: if s.checkNewOperations() != nil { return false } ... execution, err := s.Store.ClaimAndCreateStorageRepair(ctx, params)
findings.recommendation: Push the control-plane readiness predicate down into the store claim/schedule transaction, or pass a generation/readiness token that the store revalidates before inserting workflows. Apply the same pattern to controller disaster backup scheduling so the recovery barrier is enforced durably, not only by an in-process flag.
findings.impact: This weakens the recovery boundary around controller rebuild/repair scheduling. During reconciliation, user-facing APIs may already be fail-closed while background schedulers can still start fresh repair or own-state backup workflows on stale assumptions, increasing state churn exactly when the system is trying to converge.

cross_references.reason: Single-writer fence violation can reopen stale writes and requirement-closure gaps.
Recovery-state divergence affects requirement closure and is easy to regress without dedicated tests.
Background workflow churn during recovery affects both correctness and scheduler behavior.
